newsitem.title: CANADA: Effort to recreate Viking journey is abandoned.
newsitem.headline: Effort to recreate Viking journey is abandoned.

text.p: A group trying to retrace explorer Leif Ericsson's historic ocean journey to North America called off its effort on Monday but pledged to attempt it again next year.
The group, led by author-adventurer W. Hodding Carter, made its decision after their boat, a replica of Ericsson's Viking "knarr," suffered a broken rudder and had to be towed back to Greenland.

"I am disappointed. We have had to return to Greenland when we hoped to be on Baffin Island (off Canada)," Carter said in a statement from Nuuk, Greenland -- where the 54-foot (18-metre) boat will be stored for the winter.

Carter had planned to chronicle the trip retracing the 1,900-mile (3,000-km) route Ericsson took in the year 1000 from Greenland to L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland. The 12-member crew was scheduled to complete the journey by early September.
Ericsson was the first of several Viking sailors to set foot on North America, making his trip nearly 500 years before Christopher Columbus set sail.
Carter, 34, who has already retraced and written about the journeys of several U.S. historical figures, said he was inspired to attempt this trip by the adventure and history books he read as a boy.

"I believe we have learned things that have been forgotten for at least 500 years, and I believe we will learn even more in the following year," Carter said in a statement posted on the group's Internet site (http://www.viking1000.com).

The damage to the rudder could be repaired. But the group was concerned the delay would force them to sail the open ocean in worsening weather. They were already behind schedule because of light wind conditions.
Next year's trip is scheduled to start on July 1, Carter said.
The open-deck boat was powered by a single sail and six oars. It did not have an engine but carried a radio, electronic positioning equipment and crew survival suits in case of an emergency.

The project's cost of more than $500,000 was largely underwriten by retailer Lands' End. The company on Monday praised Carter's effort, but an official said it had not decided if it would fund next year's trip.
